title: Output and formatting
goal: Build a line with numbers, a character and a percent sign. Match each printf conversion to its argument.

prerequisites.text: You can build main.c, call puts and write a string in quotes.

terms.title: Format
terms.definition: A string describing ordinary text and positions for substitutions.

terms.title: Conversion specifier
terms.definition: Notation starting with %. For example %d tells printf how to print an int argument.

terms.title: Argument
terms.definition: A value passed to a function. For printf, supply the values after the format in substitution order.

sections.title: A template for a line
paragraphs: The shelf’s number, weight and section can change. A format lets you keep the ordinary text while passing the values separately. printf prints the ordinary parts as written and replaces conversion specifiers with values.

%d prints an int, %.2f prints a double with two digits after the point, and %c prints one character. The literal 'A' uses single quotes and fits %c. The string "A" is a different value and does not fit this conversion.
%% prints a percent sign and consumes no argument. printf does not add a newline automatically. Write \n in the format to end the current line.

sections.title: A shelf label
paragraphs: Before running, match the first, second and third substitutions to their arguments. Then count the arguments required for the line with the percent sign.
steps: The first %d prints 5. %.2f prints 1.25. %c prints A. Parentheses and the unit kg are ordinary text.
In the second call, %d consumes 75. %% prints %. The two notations starting with % need just one argument here.
The two \n sequences supply the line breaks. The C locale uses a point for the decimal separator. These programs leave that setting alone.
trace: Two signs in the format represent one printed sign

sections.title: A wrong type is more serious than wrong text
paragraphs: Keep argument types consistent even if the layout looks right. Using %f with the int 5 makes the type differ from what printf expects. C does not define that behaviour. If the compiler detects the mismatch, fix the type or format before running.
The letter f does not convert an integer argument to double. A newline is not printed as two characters when the string contains one backslash followed by n.

sections.title: Write a new format
paragraphs: The independent task needs a line for volume in litres and a second line for fullness. Write the format yourself. The value 2.5 requires two decimal places: 2.50.
Underline the substitutions that consume arguments. Check their order and types. Then compare the result with the specified spacing and punctuation.
Read the second line left to right: literal text, a slot for one integer, a printed percent sign, and a newline. Build the format from those parts before checking its output.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Specifies printf-family formatting and argument type requirements.

selfcheck.prompt: What is the second output line?
feedback: The number comes before the sign.

selfcheck.prompt: To display 2.50, what specifies two digits after the point?
feedback: Correct. Precision .2 gives two decimal places.
%d requires an int and prints an integer.
A newline does not change number formatting.

selfcheck.prompt: Why should %% not be matched to an argument?
selfcheck.feedback: A good explanation identifies %% as a way to print one percent sign. A number is matched to another conversion, such as %d.

practice.title: A tray label
practice.task: Print Tray 3: 2.50 L (B) followed by Fill: 80% on the next line. Pass the numbers and B as separate printf arguments. No input is needed.
criteria: The first line contains 2.50 and the second contains one % sign.
The numeric values are not written directly into the format text.
You can point to the conversion that consumes each argument.
practice.hint: The %.2f format gives two digits after the point, as the volume line requires. Use %d for the integer after Tray. To print a literal percent sign, use %%.

steps.action: Mark the argument order for both lines.
steps.why: This makes incorrect substitution easier to diagnose.
steps.expected: Identify int, double, a character and the separate second-line integer.

steps.why: The format and the arguments work together.

steps.action: Set the volume to 1.75 and the fullness to 60.
steps.why: The printed values should depend on the arguments.
steps.expected: The lines contain 1.75 and 60%, with the other layout unchanged.

exercises.title: Transfer the idea
exercises.task: Make a variant for tray 7 and section C, then change only the volume in a second run. Predict the differences before you run them.
criteria: You can point to the argument that controls each part of the result.

teaching.scene: A shelf label has three changing values: its number, mass and section letter. Assemble two lines with a fixed number of decimal places and one visible percent sign.

predict.prompt: Keep the types and order of the first printf arguments, but imagine replacing 1.25 with 3.5. How would the line change? What argument does %% need on the second line?
predict.answer: The first line becomes Shelf 5: 3.50 kg (A). The %.2f format prints two digits after the point even when the last one is zero. On the second line, %% consumes no argument, so 75 goes only into %d.

apply.prompt: A new measurement tag should show 8 3.50 C and then 40%. Which values would you supply, and how would you check the trailing zero?
apply.answer: Supply 8, 3.5 and 'C' to the three conversions on the first line. %.2f produces 3.50. For the next line, give 40 to %d%% and check for 40%.

practice.strategy: List the values with their types in output order. Select conversions in that same order, then check the number of decimal places and the percent sign.
practice.diagnosis: If 2.50 appears as 2.5, inspect the precision. If the number or letter is wrong, inspect the argument order and types first.

syntax.form:
printf("%d %.2f %c\n", whole, fraction, mark);
printf("%d%%\n", percent);
syntax.explanation: Each %d, %.2f or %c uses the next argument of the matching type. %% emits a percent sign and leaves the argument sequence untouched.
syntax.mistake: A single % starts a conversion directive. Use %% for a displayed percent sign.
